title: Composition, Lighting and Colour Words

slide.title: One Scene, Three Moods
slide.body: Three small generated images of one stone garden path: soft overcast, golden hour, lantern light at night. Small tag: AI Image Generation · Lesson 4.

production_notes: [VERSION] Test whether current Gemini, Google AI Studio and Adobe Firefly models follow hex colour codes before recording. The voiceover says generators 'often do not follow' hex codes reliably, not that none do; adjust if testing shows otherwise. Free-tier limits must also be checked.
All example images (composition, lighting and the three garden path versions) are generated by the team in Gemini from the prompts shown. No people, logos or signs with readable words in the images.
The garden path is a generic Japanese-style garden, not a named real temple or site.
Haruto and his Kyoto travel agency are fictional.
No hero B-roll: generated example images on slides carry the visuals.

Hook.voiceover: Photographers can make the same street look calm, exciting or mysterious, without moving a single object. They do it with the camera angle, the light and the colours. You can do the same with a few well-chosen words.

Explain.voiceover: In lesson two, you met the prompt formula. Today, we focus on three of its parts: composition, lighting and colour. The best words for these come from photography and design, because image models learned from many pictures described with this language.

slide.title: Composition, Lighting and Colour Words
slide.body: AI Image Generation and Visual Design · Lesson 4 of 12. The seven formula blocks, with Composition, Lighting and Colour highlighted.

Explain.voiceover: Composition words control framing and viewpoint. A close-up fills the frame with the subject, which is good for products. A medium shot shows the subject with some surroundings. A wide shot shows the whole scene, which is good for places.

slide.title: Framing
slide.body: Three generated images of the same market stall: Close-up (products fill the frame) · Medium shot (stall and some surroundings) · Wide shot (whole street, stall small).

Explain.voiceover: Then there is the camera angle. Eye level feels natural. A low angle looks up, so the subject feels large and strong. Top-down, or flat lay, looks straight down, which is popular for food. And you can ask for empty space on the left or right, to leave room for text later.

slide.title: Viewpoint
slide.body: Eye level: natural · Low angle: subject feels large and strong · Top-down / flat lay: food and products · Empty space on the left or right: room for text. Small generated example next to each.

Explain.voiceover: Lighting words control mood. Soft window light is gentle and natural. Golden hour is warm, low sunlight near sunrise or sunset. Overcast daylight is even and cool. High contrast is dramatic. And backlit means the light is behind the subject, often with a bright outline.

slide.title: Lighting words
slide.body: Soft window light: gentle · Golden hour: warm, low sun · Overcast daylight: even, cool · High contrast: dramatic · Backlit: bright outline. Each with a small generated swatch of the same cup.

Explain.voiceover: Colour words control the palette. A limited palette of two or three named colours keeps an image simple and on brand. Muted or pastel colours feel calm. Saturated colours feel energetic. And warm or cool tones change the feeling of the whole image.

slide.title: Colour words
slide.body: Limited palette of 2–3 named colours · Muted / pastel = calm · Saturated = energetic · Warm tones (orange, red, yellow) vs cool tones (blue, green)

Explain.voiceover: What about brand colours? Image generators often do not follow colour codes reliably. So describe the colour in words instead, like deep ocean blue or soft sand beige. Then correct the exact colour later in a design tool, as you will do in lesson eight.

slide.title: Brand colours in words
slide.body: Left, crossed out: '#0B5C8A'. Right, ticked: 'deep ocean blue' and 'soft sand beige' with colour swatches. Footer: fix exact values later in Canva (L08).

Explain.voiceover: Think of a small film studio. Composition, lighting and colour are the camera, the lamps and the paint. The set can stay the same, but move the camera, change the lamps or repaint the wall, and you get a different scene.
Explain.stock_query: small film studio lights and camera

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see this in practice. Haruto works for a small travel agency in Kyoto, Japan. He needs images of a quiet garden path for three different tour packages.
Demonstrate.stock_query: quiet stone garden path maple trees

Demonstrate.voiceover: His prompt is on screen. It keeps the subject, the wide shot at eye level, the empty space on the right, and a palette of green, stone grey and deep red. Only the lighting changes. There is a gap where he swaps in three different lighting phrases.

slide.title: Haruto's base prompt
slide.body:
A narrow stone path through a quiet garden with maple trees and a small wooden gate,
wide shot at eye level, empty space on the right,
[LIGHTING], limited colour palette of green, stone grey and deep red
([LIGHTING] highlighted as the only part that changes)

Demonstrate.voiceover: First, soft overcast morning light. This gives a calm, even image for a relaxing mornings tour. Second, golden hour sunlight through the leaves. Now the light is warm with long shadows, which suits an evening walks tour.

slide.title: Lighting 1 and 2
slide.body: Two generated garden path images: 'soft overcast morning light' → Relaxing mornings tour · 'golden hour sunlight through the leaves' → Evening walks tour.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Third, lantern light at night, high contrast. This gives a dark, dramatic image for a night lanterns tour. Because only one part changed, Haruto can see exactly what each lighting phrase does.

slide.title: Lighting 3
slide.body: Generated garden path image with 'lantern light at night, high contrast' → Night lanterns tour. Beside it, the first two images small, for comparison.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The three images also look related, because the subject, the composition and the palette stayed the same. And the empty space on the right is useful for the tour name and the price.

slide.title: A related set
slide.body: The three garden path images in a row, each with a placeholder tour name and price in the empty space on the right. Label: 'same subject · same composition · same palette'.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to mix words that contradict each other, like top-down and low angle, or golden hour and overcast. The model cannot show both, so it picks one, or gives you a confused image. Choose one term per category.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, words from photography, like close-up, top-down, golden hour and high contrast, give you precise control. Second, changing one part of a prompt at a time shows you what each word does. Third, describe brand colours in words, and fix exact colour values later in a design tool.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Photography words give precise control. 2. Change one part at a time to see what it does. 3. Brand colours in words; exact values later in a design tool.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below, you will generate one scene in three versions that change only the angle, the lighting or the colour, and label what each word changed. It takes about twenty minutes. In the next lesson, we learn to describe a style without copying artists. See you there.
